visual_features.color: brownish-grey upper body with darker dorsal stripe, whitish underparts, reddish-brown flanks
visual_features.body_shape: small rodent with moderately long tail, large hind feet, prominent whiskers
visual_features.distinctive_marks: spiny texture of dorsal fur, large ears, relatively long tail (about head-body length), white belly sharply demarcated
visual_features.texture: spiny to bristly fur on back, softer underparts
visual_features.pattern: agouti (banded hairs) with darker dorsal area and white belly

description: Whitehead's spiny rat, also known as Whitehead's Sundaic spiny rat, is a species of rodent in the family Muridae. It is found in Indonesia (Sumatra, Kalimantan/Borneo), Malaysia (both Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah/Sarawak), and southern Thailand. Named after the naturalist John Whitehead, this species inhabits tropical forests of Southeast Asia. Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, it faces threats primarily from habitat loss and deforestation across its range. As a small terrestrial rodent, it plays important ecological roles in forest floor ecosystems.
population_estimate: Exact population numbers are not well quantified. The species is described as uncommon to rare across its range. Population trend is decreasing due to ongoing habitat loss and deforestation in Southeast Asia.
habitat: Tropical lowland and hill forests of Sundaland (Sumatra, Borneo, Malay Peninsula). It prefers forest floor habitats with dense ground vegetation and canopy cover. Studies suggest this species prefers sites with increased ground vegetation cover and taller canopy height. It is found in primary and secondary forests but is sensitive to severe habitat disturbance.
threats: Habitat loss and deforestation across Southeast Asia
Conversion of forests to oil palm plantations
Deforestation for agriculture and timber extraction
Loss of lowland forest habitat throughout its range
ecosystem_role: As a small terrestrial rodent of the forest floor, Whitehead's spiny rat plays a role in seed dispersal and soil aeration through its burrowing and foraging activities. It serves as prey for various forest predators including snakes, birds of prey, and small carnivores, forming an important link in the tropical forest food web. Its presence indicates a healthy, functioning forest floor ecosystem.
human_connection: Like many small mammals of Southeast Asian forests, Whitehead's spiny rat is rarely seen by humans and does not typically come into direct conflict with human activities beyond the indirect effects of deforestation. Its conservation depends primarily on protecting the tropical forests where it lives.
what_students_can_do: Learn about the biodiversity of Southeast Asian rainforests
Support forest conservation organizations working in Sumatra, Borneo, and the Malay Peninsula
Study the ecology of small mammals in tropical forests
Raise awareness about the impacts of deforestation and palm oil plantations on wildlife
Promote sustainable palm oil certification (RSPO) that protects forest habitats
Understand the importance of all species in maintaining healthy ecosystems
fun_fact: The species is named after John Whitehead, a British naturalist and explorer who collected extensively in Borneo and the Philippines in the late 19th century
Whitehead's spiny rat has stiff, spiny guard hairs that give it its common name — a defense mechanism against predators
It belongs to the genus Maxomys, which includes several spiny rat species distributed across Southeast Asia
Unlike house rats (Rattus), spiny rats like Maxomys are native forest dwellers that do not thrive in human-modified environments
Studies have shown this species prefers areas with tall canopy height and dense ground vegetation cover
